Inter., 23: 165—187. The Svecofennian mobile zone occupies the bulk of the Fennoscandian shield and represents terrain subjected to profound tectonic activity and granite intrusion at —1800 My. This study covers the palaeomagnetism of basic rocks within this belt in Sweden between 65.5 and 67.5°N (gabbros and diorites of Kaliax, Niemisel, Sangis, Stora Lulevatten and the Gäuivare, Jokkmokk and Voullerim regions) magnetised during uplift and cooling of this belt at —1750—1550 My. AF and thermal demagnetisation define a consistent sequence of high to low blocking-tempera- ture components identifying a migration of the geomagnetic field during part of this interval. The Hglleforsnas giant dyke possesses a magnetite-held remanence attributed to initial cooling at 1518 My (palaeomagnetic pole 167°E, 27°N) and at least two high blocking-temperature sompo- nents. One of these is correlated with the —1000—800 My Sveconorwegian mobile activity of southwest Sweden; this latter component is represented as the univectorial remanence in dolerite dykes of this age, and sporadically as a secondary component in the adjacent Svecofennian terrain. The results are compiled with other palaeomagnetic poles from the Fennoscandian shield to derive a generalised apparent polar wandering path for the interval —1750—1550 My. They define segments of a large loop which agrees closely with uplift magnetisations from the contemporaneous Hudsonian mobile terrain of the Laurentian shield on a single reconstruction derived from Upper Proterozoic (1450—1200 My) palaeomagnetic data. The two shields thus appear to have formed an integral continental unit during the interval 1750—1200 My. A geological reconstruction of the Siberian and Laurentian shields is also tested and found to yield general agreement with the palaeomagnetic evidence. Inter., 23: 165—187. The Svecofennian mobile zone occupies the bulk of the Fennoscandian shield and represents terrain subjected to profound tectonic activity and granite intrusion at —1800 My. This study covers the palaeomagnetism of basic rocks within this belt in Sweden between 65.5 and 67.5°N (gabbros and diorites of Kaliax, Niemisel, Sangis, Stora Lulevatten and the Gäuivare, Jokkmokk and Voullerim regions) magnetised during uplift and cooling of this belt at —1750—1550 My. Two sections were sampled in the Bhittani Range, the first at Bain Pass consisting of 60 sites through 2200 m of section and the second along the North West Frontier Province Road north of Pezu consisting of 25 sites through 1000 m. Inter., 24: 142—168. Palaeomagnetic results from Precambrian rocks suggest that the geomagnetic field in the Precambrian was similar in major respects to the Recent field, although there is a possibility that reversals were less frequent. Limitations of precision in Proterozoic palaeomagnetic and geochronological data, and inadequate geographic spread of these data, prevent the making of complete Proterozoic continental reconstructions. Nevertheless, where the data are most abundant, Precambrian apparent polar wander (APW) paths can be used in determining the relative movement of cratons and groups of cratons. Relative movement between Africa, Laurentia and Australia during at least part of the Proterozoic seems to be indicated, but the lack of significant differences between the APW paths of several pairs of presently adjacent Proterozoic cratons suggests that some Proterozoic orogenic belts were not formed by the collision of previously widely separated blocks. Palaeomagnetic results from Precambrian rocks suggest that the geomagnetic field in the Precambrian was similar in major respects to the Recent field, although there is a possibility that reversals were less frequent. Limitations of precision in Proterozoic palaeomagnetic and geochronological data, and inadequate geographic spread of these data, prevent the making of complete Proterozoic continental reconstructions. Inter., 24: 142—168. Palaeomagnetic results from Precambrian rocks suggest that the geomagnetic field in the Precambrian was similar in major respects to the Recent field, although there is a possibility that reversals were less frequent. Limitations of precision in Proterozoic palaeomagnetic and geochronological data, and inadequate geographic spread of these data, prevent the making of complete Proterozoic continental reconstructions. Nevertheless, where the data are most abundant, Precambrian apparent polar wander (APW) paths can be used in determining the relative movement of cratons and groups of cratons. Relative movement between Africa, Laurentia and Australia during at least part of the Proterozoic seems to be indicated, but the lack of significant differences between the APW paths of several pairs of presently adjacent Proterozoic cratons suggests that some Proterozoic orogenic belts were not formed by the collision of previously widely separated blocks. Paleomagnetic poles for the Carboni- ferous Brush Creek limestone and Buffalo siltstone from southwestern Pennsylvania. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 25: 113—118. We report partial results of a larger project being undertaken in the Appalachian Basin to determine the character of the geomagnetic field in the Carbonjfetous. The Brush Creek limestone, which contains abundant terrigenous matter, yields reliable results from three different sites, while the overlying Buffalo siltstone appears at one locality. AF demagnetization curves, IRM acquisition curves,thermomagnetic analysis, and optical reflection microscopy indi- cate that the remanence carriers are magnetites or titanomagnetites, which are probably primary in origin. Stepwise AF demagnetization reveals that the best demagnetizing fields are 15—20 and 20—30 ml for the limestone and silt- stone units, respectively. A total of 93 specimens from 20 samples (oriented hand samples and field.drilled cores) yields a paleopole at S 36.1, W 55.7, withan alpha-95 of 4.2° and a k of 13.1 for the Brush Creek limestone. The Buffalo siltstone paleopole is located at S 27.4, W 57.0, with alpha-95 6.1° and k = 13.0 using

Kimberlite and potassic lamprophyre dykes were intensively intruded into the early Proterozoic Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt of West Greenland during an important phase of brittle reactivation in Late Precambrian-Early Cambrian times (ca. 580-570 Ma) and during at least one other minor phase. Thermal and alternating field demagnetisation studies of 52 of these dykes identify primary components residing in the critical blocking temperature range distributed between shallow westerly and steep positive directions. Near the axis of the Proterozoic shear belt the dykes (predominantly lamprophyres) have closely grouped shallow directions with a reversal; near the margins of the shear belt dykes (predominantly kimberlites) have steeper and distributed directions. The cleaned components of magnetisa- tion appear to be single, and the distribution of directions is interpreted to record a migration of the palaeofield axis which intersecting relationships show to have been from shallow to steep. The mean direction (D = 165°, I = — 10°; paleopole at 50°N 129°E) is similar to Late Carboniferous and Early Permian results. Negative fold tests, and a lack of reversals, suggest that the magnetization is secondary. However, low coercivities, low blocking temperatures, the thermomagnetic curves (Tc near 570°C) and the acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetizations all suggest that the remanence is carried by magnetite. If a detrital origin of these magnetites is assumed, the secondary nature of the remanence would argue for thermal resetting as a result of deep burial of the rocks. However, no evidence for such thermal resetting is seen in the alteration of conodonts. Four mafic and two dioritic igneous bodies intruding along the flanks of the Charlotte belt, within the King’s Mountain belt and near the Slate—Kiokee—Charlotte belt boundaries in the South Carolina Piedmont, were studied paleomagnetically. The results suggest that these mafic rocks with a single characteristic magnetization are broadly contemporaneous. A mean paleomagnetic pole position of 38.9°N 120.8°E has been calculated for the six bodies. This pole position falls near the 300 Ma old point of Irving’s apparent polar wander path (APWP) for North America. The a95 circle of confidence (10.2°) includes points on the APWP between 250—360 Ma. Anomalously old K—Ar apparent ages, greater than one billion years, are suggestive of excess 40Ar contamination for the mafic Buffalo pluton, whereas apparent ages in the range of 360—395 Ma old are interpreted as a maximum age for the other bodies, due to the possibility of small amounts of excess 40Ar being present. Palaeomagnetic evidence for the origin of Madeira. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 34: 137-149. The remanent magnetization of ' basement' volcanics from Madeira define three different axes of magnetization, each having a dual-polarity build-up. The suggested oldest of these components, with declination 302 and inclination + 4, is assigned to the late Lower Cretaceous and is thought to reflect the age of the early volcanism of the island. Subsequent magnetization overprints seem to have occurred in the Late Cretaceous/Early Tertiary (minor) and in Neogene times, respectively. The latter magnetization, which is strongly developed, was most likely impressed during the extensive volcanism that swept the island in post-Late Miocene. The palaeomagnetic evidence for a Cretaceous origin of Madeira is supported by the finding of Lower-Middle Cretaceous tuff layers in DSDP site 136 which is located only 160 km north of the island. The inferred palaeomagnetic structure of the ' basement' rocks of Madeira is similar to that found in the old volcanic complexes of other east central Atlantic islands. I. Introduction

Introduction The island of Madeira is located some 900 km southwest of Gibraltar and nearly 500 km north of the Canary Islands. In the general plate tectonic theory Madeira lies within the African plate, and according to the prevailing interpretation of marine magnetic anomalies, the crust in the Madeira re- gion formed by sea-floor spreading at around 140 Ma ago (Pitman and Talwani, 1972). Palaeomagnetism of the Foyers and Strontian granites, Scotland. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 36: 163—177. Palaeomagnetic data from the “newer granites” of Foyers and Strontian show similar directions of magnetization with southerly declinations and horizontal to intermediate, mostly downward dipping, inclinations. These palaeomagnetic directions which accord with previous data from the Helmsdale granite are thought to be of Siluro—Devonian age. The present results are not sufficiently precise to justify discussion of possible lateral displacements along the Great Glen Fault of the order of a few hundred kilometres, but it is clear that the recent idea of a c. 15_200 latitudinal offset along the Fault in the Carboniferous has to be disregarded. ble enough to have survived major folding (of probable Permian age). Nevertheless, the remanence direction (ten sites yielding a paleopole at 38.0°N, 132.4°E with dm = 3.60, dp = 1.9°). its reverse polarity and a negative intraformational conglomerate test show that the remanence was very likely acquired during the Pennsylvanian—some 130 Ma after deposition. This remanence is likely a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) acquired during diagenesis induced by heating due to deep burial under a Pennsylvanian clastic wedge. Two possible mechanisms for acquisition of CRM during deep-burial diagenesis are considered. In hypothesis 1, the oolitic hematite transformed from original goethite when heated to about 80°C, acquiring CRM. In hypothesis II, the oolitic hematite originated from ferrihydrite and was too fine-grained to acquire stable CRM until heat raised the solubility of hematite allowing grain growth. Hypothesis I explains the timing of remanence acquisition better, but there is some evidence that oolitic goethites may be stable to considerably more than 80°C. Introduction Major magmatic events in the northeastern Grampians, succeeding the Grampian erogenic event, comprise the Early Ordovician Younger Gabbros, the last Grampian granites (c. 450 Ma) and the “Newer Granites” (Bell, 1968; Pankhurst, 1970, 1974, 1979; Dewey and Pankhurst, 1970; Hurford, 1977; Pidgeon and Aftalion, 1978; Harmon and Halliday, 1980). The late Caledonian talc-alkaline “Newer Granites” were extensively emplaced in the Scottish Highlands yielding radio- metric ages dominantly in the 400-430 Ma range. In Read’s (1961) classification of Caledonian in- trusions, the “Newer Granites” were classified as the newer forceful granites and the later permitted granites, post-dating main Caledonian metamor- phism and folding. The Peterhead granite, NE Grampians (Fig. l), is intruded into metasedimen- tary rocks of the Dalradian Series presumably by stoping and fault subsidence at around 415 Ma (Whole rock Rb/Sr: Bell, 1968; Brown and Locke, 1979). The granite has subsequently been intruded by a c. 50 m thick, east-west trending dolerite dyke. The present paper forms part of a palaeomag- netic survey of “Newer Granites” and Old Red Sandstone rocks from Scotland, evaluating details in the apparent polar wander path (APW) and aspects of regional crust

Dyke samples have been collected in several profiles along the northern margin of the E-W trending dyke (south of Buchan Ness). Sampling in the contact granite was not successful due to the relatively hard and coarse- grained nature of that rock. 2. . Palaeomagnetic results from the Peterhead granite (Silurian), NE Grampian Highlands, define a characteristic magnetization with overall parameters of Dee: 180.4’, Inc: 22.3” and aas: 5.2’. These results agree with other “Newer Granite” data from North Scotland. An east-west trending dyke cutting the Peterhead granite shows an extremely well-defined palaeomagnetic direction with Dee: 192.5”, Inc: - 19.1” and aas: 1.3’, suggesting a Permo-Carboniferous age. The Peterhead Granite results are seen in conjunction with other Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Scotland. It is concluded that the observed directional spread of characteristic remanence directions previously reported from the Aberdeenshire Gabbros are not related to slow post-erogenic cooling (Watts and Briden), but is rather seen as the result of late Caledonian magnetic overprinting. 1. The Peterhead granite, NE Grampians (Fig. l), is intruded into metasedimen- tary rocks of the Dalradian Series presumably by stoping and fault subsidence at around 415 Ma (Whole rock Rb/Sr: Bell, 1968; Brown and Locke, 1979). The present paper forms part of a palaeomag- netic survey of “Newer Granites” and Old Red Sandstone rocks from Scotland, evaluating details in the apparent polar wander path (APW) and aspects of regional crustal dynamics during the Palaeozoic. These results agree with other “Newer Granite” data from North Scotland. An east-west trending dyke cutting the Peterhead granite shows an extremely well-defined palaeomagnetic direction with Dee: 192.5”, Inc: - 19.1” and aas: 1.3’, suggesting a Permo-Carboniferous age. The Peterhead Granite results are seen in conjunction with other Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Scotland. It is concluded that the observed directional spread of characteristic remanence directions previously reported from the Aberdeenshire Gabbros are not related to slow post-erogenic cooling (Watts and Briden), but is rather seen as the result of late Caledonian magnetic overprinting. 1. Thermal demagnetization studies of lavas in the Strathmore area of the Midland Valley, Scotland, support overall palaeomagnetic data found in previous studies of these rocks. Reduced directionalscatter as compared to some earlier studies, is attributed to more effective demagnetization, resolvingsome of the directional complexity of previous studies. Combined magnetic fabric and directional analysis suggest that at least some deviating directionsmay be explained by local tectonism. The existenceof almost antiparalleldirectional groups and field tests give supporting evidence for a primary” (deuteric) origin of the main magnetization of these rocks. Additionally, a second remanence component having shallow reverse directionsof magnetization, is attributed to later remagnetization in Old Red Sandstone time. The Midland Valley results are seen in conjunction with other Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results and possible geodynamicimplications are discussed. Thermal demagnetization studies of lavas in the Strathmore area of the Midland Valley, Scotland, support overall palaeomagnetic data found in previous studies of these rocks. Reduced directionalscatter as compared to some earlier studies, is attributed to more effective demagnetization, resolvingsome of the directional complexity of previous studies. Combined magnetic fabric and directional analysis suggest that at least some deviating directionsmay be explained by local tectonism. The existenceof almost antiparalleldirectional groups and field tests give supporting evidence for a primary” (deuteric) origin of the main magnetization of these rocks. Additionally, a second remanence component having shallow reverse directionsof magnetization, is attributed to later remagnetization in Old Red Sandstone time. The Midland Valley results are seen in conjunction with other Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results and possible geodynamicimplications are discussed. Introduction The eastern segment of the Appalachian orogen is largely underlain by late Precambrian (Hadrynian) rocks. Systematic mapping programs of the Avalon Zone were first undertaken by Rose (1952) and are still continuing (e.g., Nixon and Papezik, 1979). The Precambrian stratigraphy was subsequently elucidated by Rodgers (1967), Wil- liams and King (1979) and others. The Avalon Peninsula was affected by two * Present address: The Department of Geology and Geo- physics, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, ‘RN lN4, Canada. principal orogenies, a late Precambrian ‘Avalon orogeny’ (Lilly, 1966) and the ‘Acadian’ orogeny of Middle to Late Devonian age (e.g., Dallmeyer et al., 1983). Different tectonic models have been proposed for the origin of the Avalon mini-conti

Avalon Zone in Canada are a segment of a Pan-African erogenic belt incorporated into the Appalachian Orogen during Palaeozoic times as its southeast- em margin. The Avalon Zone would then be related to the Pan-African belt adjacent to the West African craton. The main objective of this 150 palaeomagnetic study and others in progress is to construct a reliable APWP for the late Pre- cambrian period in Avalonian terrane(s). 2. Palaeomagnetic data from the mafic pluton of Askoy, West Norway, suggest that its original Precambrian magnetization(s) has been completely erased by Caledonian events of regional metamorphism. The present palaeomagnetic record defines two different axes of magnetization: a predominant component carried by magnetite (the B-remanence), with Dec = 025, Ine = -22 (a95 = 4°), and a subordinate magnetization carried by haematite (the A-remanence), with Dec = 318 °, Inc ~ 8 ° (et95 ~ 10°). Comparison with Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data for NW Europe suggests that the B-magnetization was impressed in mid-Palaeozoic time, probably in the Devonian, while the A-magnetization most likely constitutes the remains of an earlier, Upper Ordovician phase of metamorphic magnetic resetting. The palaeomagnetic evidence for metamorphic events of Ordovician and Devonian ages corroborates regional structural and reconnaissance radiometric evidence. I. Introduction The

Overall palaeomagnetic results for the two magnetization axes recorded, including statistics and pole positions, are summarized in Table II. As is seen in Fig. 6 the in situ poles, A1 and B1, accord extremely well with Palaeozoic poles from Scotland (east of the Great Glen Fault) and Nor- way. Thus the A1 pole is in close correspondence to the pre-tectonic overprinted pole of Dalradian tillites (Stupavsky et al., 1982; slightly modified by Storetvedt and Deutsch, 1986) inferred to be of Upper Ordovician age (Storetvedt and Deutsch, 1986). The younger pole, B1, fits mid-Palaeozoic data, agreeing particularly well with Devonian- Lower Carboniferous poles. We believe, therefore, that the ancient magnetization, now held by the pluton, is entirely of Caledonian age, having been imposed during Upper Ordovician and Devonian events of regional metamorphism. These suggested events of Caledonian remagnetization fit the avail- able structural and radiometric evidence. All the magnetite remanence has apparently been reset during the Devonian phase, while the Ordovician palaeomagnetic component, which seems to be carried entirely by haematite, has only survived sporadically. Palaeomagnetic data from the mafic pluton of Askoy, West Norway, suggest that its original Precambrian magnetization(s) has been completely erased by Caledonian events of regional metamorphism. The present palaeomagnetic record defines two different axes of magnetization: a predominant component carried by magnetite (the B-remanence), with Dec = 025, Ine = -22 (a95 = 4°), and a subordinate magnetization carried by haematite (the A-remanence), with Dec = 318 °, Inc ~ 8 ° (et95 ~ 10°). Comparison with Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data for NW Europe suggests that the B-magnetization was impressed in mid-Palaeozoic time, probably in the Devonian, while the A-magnetization most likely constitutes the remains of an earlier, Upper Ordovician phase of metamorphic magnetic resetting. The palaeomagnetic evidence for metamorphic events of Ordovician and Devonian ages corroborates regional structural and reconnaissance radiometric evidence. I. Introduction The

Comparison with Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data for NW Europe suggests that the B-magnetization was impressed in mid-Palaeozoic time, probably in the Devonian, while the A-magnetization most likely constitutes the remains of an earlier, Upper Ordovician phase of metamorphic magnetic resetting. The palaeomagnetic evidence for metamorphic events of Ordovician and Devonian ages corroborates regional structural and reconnaissance radiometric evidence. I. Introduction The geology of the Be

1987. Paleomagnetism and rock magnetism of Early Silurian Dunn Point volcanics, Avalon Zone, Nova Scotia. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 46: 369—380. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from the subaerial volcanics (andesites, rhyolites, ignimbrites) from the Dunn Point Formation exposed in the Antigonish Highlands of the Avalon Zone, Nova Scotia. An Early Silunan age of 430 ± 15 Ma is assigned to these volcanic rocks. The age is in agreement with the fossil evidence from conformably overlying sedimentary rocks. The volcanic units were tightly folded and metamorphosed to sub-greenschist facies during one major and one secondary phase of deformation probably associated with the Mid—Late Devonian Acadian orogeny. This paleomagnetic study is based on 45 samples collected from nine sites. The site-mean directions of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) make a large deviation from the present Earth’s field with NRM intensities ranging from 10 2 to 10 Am~1. The most commonly observed remanence direction, A (D = 1530, I = —28°), obtained from both alternating fields (30—75 mT) and thermal (500—560°C) treatments yields a corresponding direction A’ (D = 0°, I = —63°) after correction for geological tilt. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from the subaerial volcanics (andesites, rhyolites, ignimbrites) from the Dunn Point Formation exposed in the Antigonish Highlands of the Avalon Zone, Nova Scotia. An Early Silunan age of 430 ± 15 Ma is assigned to these volcanic rocks. The age is in agreement with the fossil evidence from conformably overlying sedimentary rocks. The volcanic units were tightly folded and metamorphosed to sub-greenschist facies during one major and one secondary phase of deformation probably associated with the Mid—Late Devonian Acadian orogeny. The camptonite and monchiquite dykes of the Orkney Islands, intruding Middle Devonian sedimentary strata, constitute two significantly different axes of magnetization. The inferred older of these remanences has an inclination corresponding to an Upper Devonian to early Carboniferous age while the inclination of the secondary magnetization is in line with the Kiaman overprint repeatedly recorded in Orcadian Basin rocks. Middle Devonian sedimentary strata, constitute two significantly different axes of magnetization. The inferred older of these remanences has an inclination corresponding to an Upper Devonian to early Carboniferous age while the inclination of the secondary magnetization is in line with the Kiaman overprint repeatedly recorded in Orcadian Basin rocks. However, the unique palaeomagnetic property of these dykes is that both magnetizations have mean declinations of — 1700, i.e., the palaeomagnetic axes are rotated — 20 0 anticlockwise with respect to the corresponding NW European reference fields. The data represent vital new information for the discussion of transcurrent motions along the Great Glen Fault. It is concluded that the Orkney dykes originated at a late stage of an Acadian age sinistral megashear (— 600 km) at a time when the Northern Highlands block was positioned to the south of the Central Highlands. Partial remagnetization of the dykes took place at an early stage of Hercynian fault reactivation. Triassic rocks underlying the Paleogene deposits of the Ebro Basin are exposed along its SE margin. About 200 samples of Middle Triassic and Paleogene rocks from this margin have been demagnetized and analysed. The Middle Triassic red beds contain one or two secondary components of magnetization. The high unblocking temperature component has a mean direction of D 10 and I = 6 o. The Eocene red beds display a very stable magnetization. Nevertheless some samples have a high-temperature component with the present-day field direction. The Eocene mean direction is D = 220 and I = 510. The paleomagnetic results show a systematic 20 0 clockwise rotation relative to the data from the Pyrenean and Cantabrian Ranges and the western and SW part of Iberia. To explain these results two hypotheses are presented. One implies the rotation of the NE part of Iberia, whereas the other refers to a rigid block rotation mechanism along the Catalan Coastal Range. 1. Triassic rocks underlying the Paleogene deposits of the Ebro Basin are exposed along its SE margin. About 200 samples of Middle Triassic and Paleogene rocks from this margin have been demagnetized and analysed. The Middle Triassic red beds contain one or two secondary components of magnetization. The high unblocking temperature component has a mean direction of D 10 and I = 6 o. The Eocene red beds display a very stable magnetization. Nevertheless some samples have a high-temperature component with the present-day field direction. The Eocene mean direction is D = 220 and I = 510. The paleomagnetic results show a systematic 20 0 clockwise rotation relative to the data from the Pyrenean and Cantabrian Ranges and the western and SW part of Iberia. To explain these results two hypotheses are presented. One implies the rotation of the NE part of Iberia, whereas the other refers to a rigid block rotation mechanism along the Catalan Coastal Range. 1. We present palaeomagnetic evidence from Jurassic limestones and basic submarine volcanic rocks (sills, pillow lavas, and intrusive material) from the central part of the Subbetic Zone of the Betic Cordillera. Isothermal remanent magnetization acquisition experiments performed on limestones and thermomagnetic curves and measurements of the magnetic susceptibility determined for the volcanic rocks demonstrate strong dependence of rock magnetic properties on lithology. In most cases a stable magnetization could be isolated after thermal and/or alternating field demagnetiza- tion. Locally, declinations of the characteristic remanent magnetization from interbedded limestones and volcanics are similar, but inclinations tend to vary. Regionally, declinations for both limestones and volcanics show significant clockwise rotation. These results cannot be explained by the anticlockwise rotation of Iberia during the Cretaceous opening of the Bay of Biscay.

Inter., 52: 283—300. We present palaeomagnetic evidence from Jurassic limestones and basic submarine volcanic rocks (sills, pillow lavas, and intrusive material) from the central part of the Subbetic Zone of the Betic Cordillera. Isothermal remanent magnetization acquisition experiments performed on limestones and thermomagnetic curves and measurements of the magnetic susceptibility determined for the volcanic rocks demonstrate strong dependence of rock magnetic properties on lithology. In most cases a stable magnetization could be isolated after thermal and/or alternating field demagnetiza- tion. Locally, declinations of the characteristic remanent magnetization from interbedded limestones and volcanics are similar, but inclinations tend to vary. Regionally, declinations for both limestones and volcanics show significant clockwise rotation. These results cannot be explained by the anticlockwise rotation of Iberia during the Cretaceous opening of the Bay of Biscay. Permian overprints have been recognized for several years in different regions of the Hercyman chain. This process seems to affect not only large internal parts, but also external zones of the chain. Devoman limestones sampled in the Tafilalet and Maider massifs near Erfoud and Msissi reveal a strong Permian component carried mainly by magnetite. Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and X-ray investigations were performed in order to unravel the origin of this magnetite. Permian remagnetizations are also present in Visean limestones from the Meseta.

from the various intrusive units of the South Rogaland complex tend to have elongated distributions (Figs. 3-- 6) and the collective mean palaeomagnetic poles lie along a short swathe of just over 30 ° of arc incorporating the two poles from the farsundite complex at each end (Fig. 7). The pole from the Aana-Sira Massif lies at one end of the swathe, poles from the Haaland--Helleren Massifs and Bjerkrem--Sogndal lopolith lie in the middle and the poles from the Hidra and Garsaknatt bodies lie near the other end. Thus, there is a systematic trend across the basement complex, with the exception being the Aana-Sira Massif where sample blocking temperature spectra are consistently higher than those from elsewhere. The only significant exception from the calculated group means are a few sites with similar declinations, but systematically shallower inclina- tions than the remainder. There is no continuous distribution between this group of 5 sites (91, 93, 94, 63 and 66) and a separate group mean is calculat- ed as pole 'Y' in Table VII. Previous palaeomagnetic studies of the South Rogaland complex were concentrated in the northwest part of the complex, and the two outlying bodies of Hidra and Garsaknatt have not previously been sampled. Site mean directions and demagnetisation trends in the Rogaland intrusive complex define an apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) swathe of just over 30 ° of arc; poles fall along this swathe according to their position in the complex and their blocking temperatures, and the re- sultant path is interpreted as a migration of this zone away from the palaeopole at a rate of 1.3--3.0 ° Ma 1. The total swathe represents 10--20 ° of a.p.w, movement at 940--900 Ma; an isolated later ('Y') magnetisation may represent a later extension of the path at ca. 840 Ma. Two sets of magnetisations, a NW negative, predominantly hematite-held, and SSW negative, predominantly magnetite-held, are recognised in the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector and are linked to radiometric events at 1090 and 1010 Ma. In the BrattSn and AlgSn norite--anorthosite bodies of west Sweden, demagnetisa- tion trends and site mean directions define a short swathe of westerly negative directions linked to radiometric ages averaging ~ 1000 Ma. A sampling site comprises a minimum of 7 cores distributed over several metres of outcrop and drilled with a portable drilling motor of the kind de- scribed by Doell and Cox (1967). Cores were orientated by sights on the Sun or, in the limited number of cases where this was not possible, by magnetic bearings in conjunction with topographic sights. The cores were sliced in the laboratory and measured with an automated parastatic magnetometer system. Alternating field (a.f.) demagnetisation is most suitable for analysing the broad range of coercivities present in the (predominantly magnetite-held) remanences in these rocks and was utilised in increments of 5 or 10 mT (milliTesla) as the standard method of treatment for this collection. A subsequent study of the farsundite complex by Murthy and Deutsch (1975) also incorporated a test for magnetic anisotropy. Alternating field (a.f.) demagnetisation is most suitable for analysing the broad range of coercivities present in the (predominantly magnetite-held) remanences in these rocks and was utilised in increments of 5 or 10 mT (milliTesla) as the standard method of treatment for this collection. Since the rate of cooling of the migmatites surrounding the igneous com- plex is approximately known, as are the blocking temperatures of the rock samples, it is possible to estimate the rate of a.p.w, represented by the swathe in Fig. 7. Samples from the farsundite body yielding mean unblocking temperatures of 520 and 570°C have palaeopoles separated by an angular distance of 35 ° and imply an a.p.w, rate of 3 ° Ma -1. In the Aana-Sira Massif a set of samples with mean unblocking temperature of 590°C yield a pole separated by 8 ° from a set of samples in the Bjerkrem--Sogudal lopolith with a mean unblocking temperature of 565 °, implying an a.p.w, rate of 1.3 ° Ma -1. This study comprises a palaeomagnetic investigation of four areas spanning the zone: the anorthosite, farsundite and related intrusive complexes of southwest Norway, the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector bordering the Oslo Graben, the gabbro--anorthosite complex at BrattSn and ~,lgSn in west Sweden, and dolerite intrusions near the eastern tectonic front to the zone in Sweden. Site mean directions and demagnetisation trends in the Rogaland intrusive complex define an apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) swathe of just over 30 ° of arc; poles fall along this swathe according to their position in the complex and their blocking temperatures, and the re- sultant path is interpreted as a migration of this zone away from the palaeopole at a rate of 1.3--3.0 ° Ma 1. The total swathe represents 10--20 ° of a.p.w, movement at 940--900 Ma; an isolated later ('Y') magnetisation may represent a later extension of the path at ca. 840 Ma. Samples from the farsundite body yielding mean unblocking temperatures of 520 and 570°C have palaeopoles separated by an angular distance of 35 ° and imply an a.p.w, rate of 3 ° Ma -1. In the Aana-Sira Massif a set of samples with mean unblocking temperature of 590°C yield a pole separated by 8 ° from a set of samples in the Bjerkrem--Sogudal lopolith with a mean unblocking temperature of 565 °, implying an a.p.w, rate of 1.3 ° Ma -1. This study comprises a palaeomagnetic investigation of four areas spanning the zone: the anorthosite, farsundite and related intrusive complexes of southwest Norway, the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector bordering the Oslo Graben, the gabbro--anorthosite complex at BrattSn and ~,lgSn in west Sweden, and dolerite intrusions near the eastern tectonic front to the zone in Sweden. Site mean directions and demagnetisation trends in the Rogaland intrusive complex define an apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) swathe of just over 30 ° of arc; poles fall along this swathe according to their position in the complex and their blocking temperatures, and the re- sultant path is interpreted as a migration of this zone away from the palaeopole at a rate of 1.3--3.0 ° Ma 1. The total swathe represents 10--20 ° of a.p.w, movement at 940--900 Ma; an isolated later ('Y') magnetisation may represent a later extension of the path at ca. 840 Ma. This study comprises a palaeomagnetic investigation of four areas spanning the zone: the anorthosite, farsundite and related intrusive complexes of southwest Norway, the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector bordering the Oslo Graben, the gabbro--anorthosite complex at BrattSn and ~,lgSn in west Sweden, and dolerite intrusions near the eastern tectonic front to the zone in Sweden. Site mean directions and demagnetisation trends in the Rogaland intrusive complex define an apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) swathe of just over 30 ° of arc; poles fall along this swathe according to their position in the complex and their blocking temperatures, and the re- sultant path is interpreted as a migration of this zone away from the palaeopole at a rate of 1.3--3.0 ° Ma 1. The total swathe represents 10--20 ° of a.p.w, movement at 940--900 Ma; an isolated later ('Y') magnetisation may represent a later extension of the path at ca. 840 Ma. Two sets of magnetisations, a NW negative, predominantly hematite-held, and SSW negative, predominantly magnetite-held, are recognised in the gabbro--norite intrusions of the Bamble sector and are linked to radiometric events at 1090 and 1010 Ma. A sampling site comprises a minimum of 7 cores distributed over several metres of outcrop and drilled with a portable drilling motor of the kind de- scribed by Doell and Cox (1967). Cores were orientated by sights on the Sun or, in the limited number of cases where this was not possible, by magnetic bearings in conjunction with topographic sights. The cores were sliced in the laboratory and measured with an automated parastatic magnetometer system. Alternating field (a.f.) demagnetisation is most suitable for analysing the broad range of coercivities present in the (predominantly magnetite-held) remanences in these rocks and was utilised in increments of 5 or 10 mT (milliTesla) as the standard method of treatment for this collection. Thermal demagnetisation of one or more samples from many sites was, however, also undertaken using a Schonsted thermal demagnetiser to test for components ineffectively resolved by the a.f. method, but the results of this study are 205 based largely on a.f. demagnetisation and may not have comprehensively recognised components identifiable by thermal cleaning only. In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). Although the coercivity spectrum cannot of course be directly linked to the blocking temperature spectrum, similar behaviours are observed with both a.f. and thermal techniques in samples with broad spec- tra (Morgan, 1976a, b; Piper, 1981) so that the phenomenon can, at least in some rocks, be recovered by both methods. Recognition of these effects re- quires that components illustrating them are shown to have a singular and primary origin (Piper, 1981). In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). Although the coercivity spectrum cannot of course be directly linked to the blocking temperature spectrum, similar behaviours are observed with both a.f. and thermal techniques in samples with broad spec- tra (Morgan, 1976a, b; Piper, 1981) so that the phenomenon can, at least in some rocks, be recovered by both methods. Recognition of these effects re- quires that components illustrating them are shown to have a singular and primary origin (Piper, 1981). In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). Although the coercivity spectrum cannot of course be directly linked to the blocking temperature spectrum, similar behaviours are observed with both a.f. and thermal techniques in samples with broad spec- tra (Morgan, 1976a, b; Piper, 1981) so that the phenomenon can, at least in some rocks, be recovered by both methods. Recognition of these effects re- quires that components illustrating them are shown to have a singular and primary origin (Piper, 1981). In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. The site mean directions from this study form elongate distributions (Figs. 3--6) with palaeopoles which approximately parallel the swathe of group mean direc- tions, and cores from the two intrusive units showing the lowest ranges of blocking temperatures (the Garsaknatt body and the northern part of the farsundite body) exhibit progressive movement SSE or parallel to this swathe. As both a.f. and thermal demagnetisation have the resultant effect of selectively removing the magnetisations residing in grains with lower blocking temperatures, this movement may indicate a migration from younger to older palaeopoles. This interpretation is suggested by the observa- tions that the great circles defined by the movement incorporate neither the present field direction nor the predominant Caledonian palaeofield direction, and it is essentially confirmed by the distribution of high to low blocking temperature components: the blocking temperature of the rocks of the Aana-Sira Massif, as defined by the thermal demagnetisation studies, are higher than the other intrusive units of the South Rogaland complex. In both cases the implied direction of a.p.w, is away from the sam- pling locality (Fig. 7). Since the rate of cooling of the migmatites surrounding the igneous com- plex is approximately known, as are the blocking temperatures of the rock samples, it is possible to estimate the rate of a.p.w, represented by the swathe in Fig. 7. Samples from the farsundite body yielding mean unblocking temperatures of 520 and 570°C have palaeopoles separated by an angular distance of 35 ° and imply an a.p.w, rate of 3 ° Ma -1. In the Aana-Sira Massif a set of samples with mean unblocking temperature of 590°C yield a pole separated by 8 ° from a set of samples in the Bjerkrem--Sogudal lopolith with a mean unblocking temperature of 565 °, implying an a.p.w, rate of 1.3 ° Ma -1. These estimates are appreciably higher than most Phanerozoic rates, but appear to be fairly typical of the Phanerozoic era (Piper, 1981, 1982). The Cheneaux metagabbro (Helikian) is a slightly to moderately metamorphosed intrusive body in the southern Grenville province. The paleomagnetic study undertaken on it yielded 3 main components of magnetization. V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of amphibolite and granulite facies base- ment rocks across a 60 km wide north--south traverse through the Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt in West Greenland, which incorporates the c. 2500 Ma Itivdleq shear belt, the c. 1800 Ma Ikert6q shear belt, and adjoining terrains. Progressive a.f. and thermal cleaning of samples from 81 sites identifies a range of magnetic components. Lowest blocking temperature remanences in Nagssugtoqidian (c. 1700 Ma) amphibolite facies rocks yield steep W to N positive components residing in magnetite. V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of amphibolite and granulite facies base- ment rocks across a 60 km wide north--south traverse through the Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt in West Greenland, which incorporates the c. 2500 Ma Itivdleq shear belt, the c. 1800 Ma Ikert6q shear belt, and adjoining terrains. It also integrates the results with earlier investigations of the belt to produce a composite record of the magnetic field during uplift and cooling of the terrain through c. 600--500°C at c. 1750--1600 Ma. Progressive a.f. and thermal cleaning of samples from 81 sites identifies a range of magnetic components. Lowest blocking temperature remanences in Nagssugtoqidian (c. 1700 Ma) amphibolite facies rocks yield steep W to N positive components residing in magnetite. Granulite facies rocks formed at c. 1800 Ma generally have a dual record incor- porating steep N to NW positive components unblocked by 580°C and shallow E--W di- rected components of dual polarity only unblocked close to the Curie point of haematite. V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the
